per_question.question: What's the core functional difference between reserved concurrency and provisioned concurrency in Lambda?

The core functional difference between them is that reserved concurrency sets a fixed number of execution environments exclusively for a function, while provisioned concurrency sets a fixed number of pre-initialized execution environments that are ready to respond immediately to incoming function requests.

In other words, reserved concurrency acts as a cap on the maximum and minimum number of concurrent instances allocated to a function, while provisioned concurrency allows a function to use a fixed number of pre-initialized execution environments, which can improve response times and reduce cold start latencies.

per_question.question: Lambda SnapStart and provisioned concurrency both exist to reduce cold-start latency, but you can't enable both on the same function version. Using what each mechanism actually does, explain why they're mutually exclusive and which runtimes get the free option.
per_question.gold_source_doc: Core concepts > Running code ; Function scaling > Understanding reserved and provisioned concurrency
per_question.generated_answer:
Lambda SnapStart and provisioned concurrency both aim to reduce cold-start latency, but they work in different ways and are mutually exclusive because they require different execution environments.

Lambda SnapStart uses cached snapshots of the execution environment to significantly improve startup performance. This means that when a function is invoked, Lambda uses a pre-existing environment that has already been set up, which reduces the time it takes to start executing the function. However, this approach requires that the function is not using provisioned concurrency, because provisioned concurrency would require Lambda to create a new environment from scratch.

On the other hand, provisioned concurrency pre-provisions execution environments for your function before it starts receiving requests. This means that when a function is invoked, it can use a pre-existing environment that has already been set up, which reduces the time it takes to start executing the function. However, this approach requires that the function is using provisioned concurrency, because it needs a pre-existing environment to draw from.

Since Lambda SnapStart and provisioned concurrency require different execution environments, they cannot be enabled on the same function version. The free option, Lambda SnapStart, is available for Java 11 and Java 17 runtimes, which means that functions written in these runtimes can take advantage of the improved startup performance without incurring additional costs.

In summary, Lambda SnapStart and provisioned concurrency are mutually exclusive because they require different execution environments, and the free option, Lambda SnapStart, is available for Java 11 and Java 17 runtimes.

Citations: [1], [2]
per_question.ideal_answer: SnapStart reduces cold starts by resuming new execution environments from a persisted, encrypted memory-and-disk snapshot taken during a special Restore phase, instead of running full initialization from scratch. Provisioned concurrency reduces cold starts by keeping a specified number of execution environments pre-initialized and ready in advance. Because both are alternative solutions to the same cold-start problem, Lambda doesn't allow configuring them together on one function version. SnapStart is available at no extra cost for the Java 11 and Java 17 runtimes, while provisioned concurrency incurs additional charges regardless of runtime.

This allows you to specify exactly which services and resources are allowed to invoke your function, and under what conditions.

On the other hand, the execution role's trust policy is scoped to the service that assumes the role, and it only includes the necessary permissions to perform the assumed role's actions. While this provides a good level of security, it can be less flexible than a custom policy defined with PutResourcePolicy.

In contrast, AddPermission is a simpler way to grant access to another service, but it is limited to a single action (InvokeFunction) and does not allow for the same level of customization as PutResourcePolicy.
